title: The LLM gateway
bridge: The gateway is like a backend-for-frontend that holds the API key your React app must never see. Except it never reads or changes the body: it streams the bytes through and only counts the usage numbers.
intro: Every Claude call from an agent goes through one small service of ours. It checks a run token, adds the Anthropic key for that workload, streams the answer back, and counts tokens and dollars. This lesson builds it in TypeScript, meters it, and deploys it on inf-rhinohealth.

picture.caption: One call from a sandbox VM. The gateway swaps the run token for the workload's key, streams the answer back untouched, and only counts the usage.

steps.text: POST /v1/messages with Authorization: Bearer <run token> and x-ai-agents-step
verifies the HMAC signature, expiry and epoch; a bad token gets 401
gives the key for the token's workload (nova, routines or brain-bot)
forwards the same body and path with x-api-key added
the SSE stream flows back through a tap that reads only the usage events
ai_agents_llm_tokens_total and ai_agents_llm_cost_usd_total are scraped every 30 seconds
a day above 2x the 14-day average posts to #ai-agents-alerts

sections.h: What the VM is given instead of a key
p: Look at the session options from lesson p8-1. In the VM, nova-worker starts a session with ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=https://llm-gateway.example.com and ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN set to a run token. There is no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY anywhere on that machine.

The gateway is our service that adds the Anthropic key and meters spend. It is a reverse proxy: a server that receives a request, forwards it to another server, and returns the answer. Anthropic's hosting guide recommends exactly this shape, a proxy that injects the key.

A run token is a short signed string the orchestrator mints for one run. It names the agent, the Jira key, the run and an expiry, and it dies with the run. It is not an Anthropic key, so a leaked token leaks nothing that lasts.

callout.text: No keys in the VM. The three workload keys from lesson g0-2 are read by the gateway pod only, and the gateway never writes them anywhere.

sections.h: The token, the epoch and the kill switch
p: src/auth.ts signs tokens with createHmac("sha256") and a signing key stored at kvv2 infrastructure/ai-agents/gateway. An HMAC is a hash of the token body mixed with a secret. Only a holder of the secret can make a valid signature. The check uses timingSafeEqual, which compares in constant time, so nobody can measure how many bytes matched.

Each token also carries an epoch: a number the gateway keeps per agent. Bump an agent's epoch and every live token of that agent stops working. A disabled_agents setting refuses an agent outright. Together they are the kill switch.
src/mint-token.ts mints a token for tests. In production the orchestrator mints one per run with the same signing key, which G3-17 gives it through Vault.
The block below is the lab's stub of auth.ts, not the real file. It shows the HMAC in 20 lines and leaves out the epoch and disabled_agents checks.
sections.because: We sign the token instead of storing it, because the gateway can then check it with one secret and no database.

notes.text: createHmac makes the signature; timingSafeEqual compares two buffers in constant time.
The five claims every token carries. exp is a Unix time in seconds.

An expired token is refused. The real file also checks the agent's epoch and the disabled_agents setting.

p: The file is 35 lines, so we read it as two blocks. This block holds the imports and four constants. Nothing runs yet. Only the file-path comment line is dropped from the sketch.

Node's global fetch is built on undici. We import undici's Agent only to set waits: 10 seconds to connect, then 15 minutes between header bytes and between body bytes. Each wait restarts on every byte, so a stream can run for hours. There is no total limit, by design.
sections.because: We set per-wait limits and never a total, because no limit may cut a run in the middle.

The waits in milliseconds: 10 s to connect, 900 s between bytes. Per wait, never a total.
The rule in one line: over budget is not a reason to refuse. 429 and 529 pass through.

callout.text: On the laptop, npm's undici is a different copy from the one inside Node's global fetch. That fetch refuses an Agent from another copy and fails with 'fetch failed'. The lab imports fetch from undici too. The ticket should do the same, or pin undici to the version Node 24 bundles.

sections.h: server.ts, part 2: one request end to end
p: This block is the handler. Read it top to bottom as one request: health, route, token, forward, stream back.
The body goes through untouched. The only thing in the middle is a Transform called tap, which hands each chunk to the meter and passes it on. The meter reads usage numbers; it never keeps text.
sections.because: We stream through a pass-through rather than buffering, because the harness needs the first token at once.

notes.text: One async handler for every request.
Parse the path. The base URL is only there to parse; url.search keeps the query string for the forward.
GET /health answers ok for the pod's readiness and liveness probes.
Anything that is not a POST to one of the two routes is 404.
Check the run token from the Authorization header. A missing, expired or revoked token throws RunTokenError.
Collect the forwarded request headers that are present, as a plain object.
fetch to api.anthropic.com with the same path and query string.
The whole body, read with buffer, and the undici dispatcher with the long waits.
x-api-key is the workload's key. accept-encoding: identity keeps the bytes plain, so the meter can read them.
Write the upstream status and the allowed response headers back. 429 and 529 go through here with retry-after.
A Meter for this call, tagged with the x-ai-agents-step header that G1-14 sets, or unknown.
The tap: every chunk goes to meter.feed and then on to the client, unchanged.

Pipe upstream body to tap to response. finally closes the meter, so counts are written even after an error. The cast to ReadableStream is needed: without it tsc fails with @types/node 24 and TypeScript 5.9.
A bad token is 401; anything else is 502. Only if no headers were sent yet.
Listen on 8080. The access log holds method, path, status and latency only; no body is ever logged.

callout.text: The G0-13 ticket sketch calls Readable.fromWeb(up.body) with no cast. With @types/node 24 and TypeScript 5.9 that fails tsc, because fetch's body type and Node's web stream type do not match. Cast it as above, with the type imported from node:stream/web (lesson p1-2).

sections.h: Rules the gateway keeps, and a fake upstream
p: Three rules shape the rest of the ticket. First, never touch content: no body logging, and a node:test case in gateway/test/server.test.ts fails if any request text reaches the logs. Second, pass 429 and 529 through with retry-after; the harness waits and retries. Third, the gateway never refuses a call over budget.

The image is ai-agents-llm-gateway, built by ai-agents/.github/workflows/images.yml like Byte's Dockerfile. FROM node:24-bookworm-slim pinned by digest, npm ci --ignore-scripts, a tsc build, non-root user 10001 and CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]. Port 8080 serves the API and 9090 serves metrics.

On the client side the harness sets ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL and ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN, plus ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=true and CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FINE_GRAINED_TOOL_STREAMING=1. Both are off by default behind a gateway. Test with claude -p and with the Agent SDK, streaming and not.
To test on a laptop we need an upstream that costs nothing. The block below is the lab's fake Anthropic. It answers POST /v1/messages with three SSE events and the usage numbers the meter reads.

callout.text: Request bodies are read whole with no 1 MiB cap, unlike Byte's broker. A long session sends several MB per call, and Anthropic caps the size itself.

sections.because: We test against a fake upstream, because the lab must never spend money or hold a company key.

sections.h: meter.ts, part 1: counters and the stream
p: The meter answers two questions: how many tokens, and how many dollars, per agent, model, Jira key, run and step. It exports them as Prometheus counters, as in lesson p6-2: numbers that only go up, read by a scraper. The library is @prometheus-io/client, prom-client's new name with the same API.

A streamed response is SSE, server-sent events: plain text, a few lines per event, events separated by a blank line. Two events carry usage. In message_start the usage sits inside message; in message_delta the output_tokens is a running total. A non-streaming call returns one JSON object instead.
This block is 17 lines: the counters, the fields and feed(). The library does not add _total to names, so the names carry it.
sections.because: We read usage from the response rather than counting tokens ourselves, because Anthropic's numbers are the ones on the invoice.

notes.text: createServer again, for the metrics port at the end of part 2.
Counter and the default register from @prometheus-io/client.
RunClaims is the type of the verified token: agent, jira, run, exp, epoch.
pricePerMtok(model, type) reads prices.yaml: dollars per million tokens.
Tokens by agent, model, token type and step. The name ends in _total because the library does not add it.
Cost by agent, model, Jira key, run and step. The run label is fine at a few hundred runs a month.
The three shapes in one type: message_start nests under message, the others do not.
The class reads only usage numbers. Text is never kept or logged.
Private fields: the model, the usage so far, a buffer for a half-received event, and a streaming UTF-8 decoder.
The constructor takes the claims and the step name.
feed is called by the tap in server.ts for every chunk.
Join the leftover text and the new chunk, then split on blank lines: one piece per SSE event.
The last piece may be half an event. Keep it for the next chunk.
Only data: lines that mention usage are parsed. Every other line is dropped unread.

sections.h: meter.ts, part 2: prices and the metrics port
p: #take merges the usage fields of one event into #usage, so message_delta's running total overwrites message_start's early number. close() runs once, when the stream ends, and turns the totals into counter increments.

Prices live in ai-agents/gateway/prices.yaml, loaded by src/prices.ts with the yaml package, in dollars per million tokens. Opus 5.5: input 4, output 20, cache write 5 for 5 minutes or 8 for 1 hour, cache read 0.20. Sonnet 5.5: 2, 10, 2.50 or 4, 0.10. Haiku 5.5: 0.10, 0.50, 0.125 or 0.20, 0.01, up to 100K-token prompts.

An unknown model still counts tokens and raises an alert; the call never fails. GET /v1/spend?run=… or ?jira=… answers from VictoriaMetrics through a fetch to vmselect at SPEND_QUERY_URL, so totals survive a restart. A 30-second scrape delay is fine for a backstop checked between turns.
sections.because: We split cache writes into 5-minute and 1-hour because they have different prices, and G1 reads them back as one cache_write type.

notes.text: #take gets one parsed event or body.
message_start nests the message; message_delta and a plain JSON body do not.
Keep the model from the event, or the one we already have.
Copy every integer field: input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_creation_input_tokens, cache_read_input_tokens.
1-hour cache writes sit deeper, in usage.cache_creation.ephemeral_1h_input_tokens.
Store them under cache_write_1h; they cost more than 5-minute writes.
close runs once, from the finally in server.ts.
A non-streaming call: the whole JSON body is still in the buffer, so parse it now.
The labels shared by both counters, from the claims and the step.
5-minute writes are all cache writes minus the 1-hour ones. The other parts are copied as they are.
One increment per token type. The suffix is stripped, so G1 sees type=cache_write for both.
Cost is the sum of count times price, divided by one million.
The cost increment carries jira and run too, so the weekly review can sum per ticket.
A second node:http server answers every request with the metrics text in Prometheus format.
Port 9090, apart from the API on 8080, so the scraper never touches the API port.

sections.h: The Terragrunt unit, part 1: module and inputs
p: The gateway runs on inf-rhinohealth as a Terraform helm_release unit, like n8n in lesson p4-2. A unit is one folder with one terragrunt.hcl that points at a module and gives it inputs. This one is infrastructure/multi_tenant/accounts/infrastructure/ai-agents/llm-gateway/terragrunt.hcl.

The module is new in this ticket: modules/ai-agents-service, a small local chart shaped like modules/goalert/chart. It holds a Deployment, a Service, an HTTPRoute, an ExternalSecret from vault-store and a VMServiceScrape. A VMServiceScrape tells VictoriaMetrics which port to scrape. G3's broker, workers and Slack app reuse it.

Pods keep the image's command, run as user 10001 with a read-only root filesystem, and probe GET /health. First, DevOps adds the ECR repo ai-agents-llm-gateway with tags_immutability_enabled = true to multi_tenant/accounts/infrastructure/artifacts/artifacts.hcl. The ai-agents repo's images.yml builds and pushes the image.
sections.because: We deploy through a unit and a shared module, because the next four services need the same shape.

notes.text: Include the shared root.hcl found in a parent folder: remote state, providers and tags.
expose = true lets this file read include.root.locals, used for the metrics namespace in part 2.
The module path in the old tree, five folders up. The double slash marks where the module root starts.
Every input becomes a value for the chart.
Name and namespace: llm-gateway in the ai-agents namespace.
The image from inf ECR at a tag. CMD node dist/server.js comes from the image itself.
Two replicas, fixed. KEDA is off on inf.
8080 is the API port the Service exposes.
9090 is the port the VMServiceScrape reads.
GET /health for readiness and liveness; user 10001 and a read-only root filesystem come from the module.

sections.h: The Terragrunt unit, part 2, and the alert
p: The second half wires secrets, one env var and the route. The ExternalSecret reads two Vault paths through the existing ClusterSecretStore vault-store: the three workload keys and the token-signing key. An HTTPRoute is the Envoy Gateway resource that gives the service a hostname. envoy-internal means VPN, Teleport and in-cluster callers only.

The route's request timeout is 0s. n8n sets 300s; a stream with 64K to 128K output tokens runs for many minutes and would be cut. How sandbox VMs reach the gateway without VPC peering is a G3 decision, and the comment in the file says so.

Then the alert. Add victoria-metrics/alerting/templates/alert_rules/ai-agents.yml with AIAgentDailySpendUnusual: sum by (agent) (increase(ai_agents_llm_cost_usd_total[1d])) above 2x its 14-day average. Route service.name=ai-agents to a new Slack receiver for #ai-agents-alerts. A person runs plan and apply. The smoke test is claude -p 'say ok' through the gateway from a pod, then its cost series in Grafana.
sections.because: We set the route timeout to zero, because a long stream must not be cut by the thing in front of it.

notes.text: The ClusterSecretStore vault-store already exists on inf; the module makes one ExternalSecret from it.
Two kvv2 paths: anthropic holds the three workload keys from G0-07, gateway holds the token-signing key.
SPEND_QUERY_URL points /v1/spend at vmselect in the metrics namespace, read from the root locals.
The route block becomes the HTTPRoute.
envoy-internal: reachable from VPN, Teleport and inside the cluster only, in v0.
The hostname is the harness's ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL.
0s means no route timeout. n8n's 300s would cut a long stream.
The open decision for G3: PrivateLink, or envoy-external with the WAF behind the egress proxy.

callout.text: The alert does not stop anything. Someone hears about a runaway day before the invoice; the harness backstop in G3 stays in shadow mode for 4 weeks.

quiz.q: A run has spent past its far-away backstop. What does the gateway do with the next call?

options.text: Returns 429 with retry-after so the harness slows down.
options.why: 429 only passes through from Anthropic. The gateway never makes its own refusal over budget.

options.text: Serves it and counts it; the harness decides between turns, in shadow mode for 4 weeks.
options.why: The gateway reports and never refuses. No limit cuts a run in the middle.

options.text: Bumps the agent's epoch so the token dies.
options.why: The epoch is the kill switch for a misbehaving agent, not a budget tool.

quiz.q: Where does the Anthropic key live while a run is going?

options.text: In the VM, as ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in the harness environment.
options.why: No keys in the VM. The VM only holds ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN, the run token.

options.text: Inside the run token, encrypted with the signing key.
options.why: The token carries agent, jira, run, exp and epoch. The gateway looks the key up by agent.

options.text: In the gateway pod, mounted from Vault through an ExternalSecret.
options.why: vault_secret_paths lists infrastructure/ai-agents/anthropic; workloadKey reads the mount.

quiz.q: Why is request_timeout set to 0s on the gateway's HTTPRoute?

options.text: A stream with 64K to 128K output tokens runs for many minutes; n8n's 300s would cut it.
options.why: A long stream must not be cut by the thing in front of it. The undici waits are per byte, never a total.

options.text: 0s means use the Envoy default, which is enough.
options.why: 0s turns the route timeout off. The default would still cut long streams.

options.text: The health probes fail with any timeout set.
options.why: GET /health answers at once; the probes are not the reason.
